exam: IISER Aptitude Test (IAT) 2027 preparation — provisional 2026-pattern pilot
title: IAT New Test 13
review_status: fresh AI-assisted authoring; independent academic review pending
notification_source: Official IAT 2026 examination page and 2026 Information Brochure, sections 19 and 23; a 2027 brochure has not been verified
past_paper_reference: 539 English archive entries from 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021–2026; 2026 key provisional; analysed for topic/style only, no questions copied
authoring_source: Individually authored TSV records against the 25-test slot plan; mechanical assembly only; academic review pending
order_policy: fixed authored order; do not shuffle questions or options or renumber image-linked IDs
instructions: This is an original preparation pilot for manual review, based on the verified 2026 scheme; it is not an official IAT paper or a verified 2027 notification.
There are 60 single-correct questions: Biology 1–15, Chemistry 16–30, Mathematics 31–45 and Physics 46–60.
Each question has exactly one correct option. Correct: +4; incorrect: -1; unanswered: 0. All questions are available to attempt; there is no best-three-subject scoring rule.
Use 180 minutes. An on-screen non-programmable scientific calculator is part of the 2026 examination conditions; personal calculators are not allowed under that scheme.
Treat stated data and idealisations as exact unless an approximation is explicitly supplied. Log denotes base 10 and ln denotes the natural logarithm.
The review PDF contains the question paper first, followed by a separate answer key and worked solutions. Keep the solutions hidden during a timed attempt.

difficulty_policy.basis: user-directed editorial mix, not measured item difficulty

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A microscopic specimen in the figure has chlorophyll a and b and stores starch within a chloroplast. Which algal group is most consistent with these linked traits?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Green algae.
Why: Green algae commonly possess chlorophyll a and b and store starch associated with chloroplasts. Pigment plus reserve product is stronger evidence than colour alone because lighting or age can alter appearance.
Why not the others: (B) brown algae have fucoxanthin and laminarin; (C) red algae use phycobilins and floridean starch; (D) are prokaryotic and lack chloroplasts.
Key point: Combine pigment and reserve traits.
questions.image_alt: Chloroplast pigments and starch storage evidence

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: The flower diagram shows a superior ovary with sepals, petals and stamens attached below it. Which position is represented?
options: D) Inferior ovary with epigynous insertion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Hypogynous.
Why: The other whorls arise below a superior ovary, the defining spatial arrangement of a hypogynous flower. A cup-like insertion around, but not above, a free ovary would instead support perigyny.
Why not the others: (A) epigynous insertion places whorls above an inferior ovary; (C) perigynous insertion places them around a cup; (D) explicitly names an inferior ovary contrary to the diagram.
Key point: Locate the insertion relative to ovary base.
questions.image_alt: Superior ovary and whorl attachment points

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A eukaryotic messenger RNA leaves the nucleus and is translated into a secreted protein. Where does translation begin and where does elongation proceed after the signal peptide is recognised?
options: C) Cytosolic ribosome, then ribosome associated with rough ER
D) Golgi lumen, then plasma membrane
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Cytosol to rough ER.
Why: Protein synthesis starts on cytosolic ribosomes; a signal sequence directs the translating ribosome to the ER membrane, allowing the nascent secretory chain to enter the ER. The RNA is not translated within the nucleus.
Why not the others: (A) the nucleus processes RNA but does not host the described translation; (B) mitochondria do not initiate this nuclear-encoded secretory route; (D) Golgi modifies cargo after ER synthesis rather than translating mRNA.
Key point: Signal recognition redirects an ongoing translation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the Calvin cycle, three CO₂ molecules are fixed. How many molecules of the three-carbon triose phosphate leave the cycle as the net carbohydrate product while the rest regenerate RuBP?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) One net triose.
Given: Three CO₂ add three carbons to the cycle.
Formula/Principle: Six triose phosphates form transiently; five regenerate three RuBP molecules.
Step 1: Six minus five gives one net three-carbon triose.
Why: The six immediate reduction products are not six exported products: most carbon must recycle into the acceptor to keep fixation going. The three fixed carbon atoms leave as one net three-carbon product, while the other five triose units recycle their carbon skeletons to regenerate the acceptor.
Why not the others: (A) counts RuBP molecules; (B) assumes a glucose product from three CO₂; (C) counts all transient trioses.
Key point: Distinguish gross intermediate formation from net export.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A contracting sarcomere shortens while thin and thick filaments keep their own lengths. Which pair of band changes is expected?
options: A) I band narrows, A band remains approximately constant
B) A band narrows, I band remains constant
C) Both bands narrow in proportion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) I band narrows; A band persists.
Why: Sliding filament overlap increases without shortening the myosin thick filament, whose length sets the A band. The thin-only region at each sarcomere end shrinks, reducing I-band width.
Why not the others: (B) reverses bands; (C) assumes filament shortening; (D) ignores changing overlap.
Key point: Band widths reflect filament lengths and overlap differently.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In an angiosperm cross, the maternal sporophyte is 2n=24 and paternal pollen-producing plant is also 2n=24. Assuming normal haploid gametes, what are embryo and endosperm chromosome numbers after double fertilisation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 24 and 36.
Given: Egg, each polar nucleus and each sperm have n=12.
Formula/Principle: Embryo=egg+sperm; primary endosperm nucleus=two polar nuclei+second sperm.
Step 1: Embryo 12+12=24; endosperm 12+12+12=36.
Why: The two sperm participate in different fusion events, and central-cell maternal contribution includes two haploid nuclei. Embryo and endosperm therefore have different ploidy even though both fertilisation events use sperm from the same pollen grain.
Why not the others: (A) omits a polar nucleus; (C) swaps tissues; (D) omits sperm contribution to embryo.
Key point: Track each nucleus in each fusion.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a replication fork moving right, the upper parental template is read 3′→5′ toward the fork. Which statement describes new synthesis on that template?
options: A) The strand is made 3′→5′ continuously
B) The strand is made 5′→3′ only as short fragments away from fork
C) The leading strand grows 5′→3′ toward the fork
D) No DNA can be made on this template
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Continuous leading synthesis.
Why: Polymerase reads a template 3′→5′ and extends the daughter strand 5′→3′. When the template orientation points into fork movement, extension follows the fork and can be continuous.
Why not the others: (A) reverses polymerase chemistry; (B) describes the lagging configuration; (D) ignores complementary directionality.
Key point: Align template reading direction with fork travel.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: After primary vaccination, antibody titre rises slowly. A booster after several months produces a faster, larger rise. Which claim is best supported by these two curves?
options: A) Booster creates all antigen-specific cells from scratch
B) The first dose cannot generate memory
C) The booster changes antibody gene sequences by design
D) Memory-cell response accelerates secondary production compared with naive exposure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Faster secondary response reflects memory.
Why: A controlled repeat exposure to the same antigen elicits a shorter lag and stronger titre, consistent with expansion of antigen-experienced B cells and helper responses. The curves alone do not imply instantaneous protection or permanent titre at every later time.
Why not the others: (A) ignores primed antigen-specific cells from the first dose; (B) denies the memory needed to explain the shorter lag; (C) assumes a deliberately engineered antibody sequence not established by the curves.
Key point: Compare response lag and magnitude, not only peak height.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A linear double-stranded DNA target is shown with top strand 5′ at left and 3′ at right. Which primer orientation permits amplification of the interval between the two inward-facing sites?
options: A) Left forward primer extends right; right reverse primer extends left
D) Both primers anneal with 3′ ends pointing outward
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Primers must face each other.
Why: DNA polymerase extends each primer from its 3′ end in the 5′→3′ direction. For exponential amplification of the bounded interval, extension from the left site proceeds right and from the right site proceeds left on opposing templates.
Why not the others: (B) sends both extensions in one direction, so one flank is not copied inward; (C) reverses that common direction but still leaves a flank; (D) points both free 3′ ends away from the interval.
Key point: Read the direction of each primer's free 3′ end.
questions.image_alt: Inward-facing DNA primers on antiparallel strands

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A grassland fixes 1400 kJ m⁻² day⁻¹ as gross primary productivity and autotrophs respire 500 kJ m⁻² day⁻¹. Herbivores assimilate 120 kJ m⁻² day⁻¹. What is plant net primary productivity?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 900 kJ m⁻² day⁻¹.
Given: Gross productivity includes plant respiration.
Formula/Principle: NPP=GPP−autotrophic respiration.
Step 1: 1400−500=900.
Why: The herbivore assimilation is a later transfer of produced plant matter, not a term subtracted from the definition of plant NPP. Consumer assimilation may later affect ecosystem energy transfers, but it does not enter the gross-minus-plant-respiration definition used here.
Why not the others: (A) is herbivore assimilation; (C) adds it; (D) adds respiration.
Key point: Separate production from consumer uptake.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In an inducible bacterial operon, a functional repressor blocks transcription without inducer. The operator DNA is mutated so that the repressor can no longer bind, while coding genes remain intact. What happens in absence of inducer?
options: B) Only translation, not transcription, changes
D) The repressor protein itself is deleted
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Operator escape permits transcription.
Why: The operator is a DNA binding site; eliminating repressor binding removes this negative gate while retaining functional structural genes and repressor protein. Other regulatory factors can still modulate output, so the inference is permission for constitutive expression under the model.
Why not the others: (A) predicts opposite effect; (B) ignores DNA-level transcription control; (D) confuses site mutation with protein deletion.
Key point: Distinguish a regulator from its binding site.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An mRNA reading frame begins AUG–GAA–UAA. If translation begins at the first AUG, how many amino acids are incorporated before termination?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Two.
Why: AUG codes methionine and initiates; GAA codes glutamate; UAA is a stop signal and does not add an amino acid. The reading frame is stipulated to avoid ambiguity from an upstream start.
Why not the others: (A) overlooks GAA; (B) counts stop as an amino acid; (C) counts nucleotides as codons.
Key point: A stop codon ends translation without coding a residue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two patients have similarly low circulating thyroid hormone. Patient P has high TSH; patient Q has low TSH. Which distinction is most consistent with intact negative feedback in P and impaired pituitary drive in Q?
options: A) Neither can have thyroid disease
B) P has pituitary failure, Q has primary thyroid failure
C) Both necessarily have iodine excess
D) P has primary thyroid failure, Q may have secondary pituitary failure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) High versus low TSH localises the fault.
Why: Low thyroid output relieves inhibitory feedback, so an intact pituitary should raise TSH in primary gland failure. A low TSH despite low thyroid hormone points upstream to deficient pituitary stimulation under the stated alternatives; a hypothalamic cause remains another upstream possibility.
Why not the others: (A) contradicts low hormone; (B) reverses the response; (C) is unsupported by the paired measurements.
Key point: Interpret a hormone together with its upstream controller.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A diploid cell has 2n=8 and 2C DNA in G1. At metaphase after replication but before sister chromatids separate, how many chromosomes and how much DNA does it contain?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Eight chromosomes and 4C DNA.
Given: Chromosome count tracks centromeres, and chromatids remain joined.
Formula/Principle: S phase doubles DNA mass but not chromosome number.
Step 1: G1 8 and 2C becomes metaphase 8 duplicated chromosomes and 4C.
Why: Each of the eight chromosomes now has two sister chromatids; the latter are not counted as separate chromosomes until centromeres divide. At anaphase sister centromeres separate, which is the later event that changes chromosome counting within the same cell.
Why not the others: (A) prematurely counts chromatids; (C) misses DNA duplication; (D) combines both errors.
Key point: Count centromeres separately from DNA amount.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A DNA digest gel has a 900 bp band in lane X and 600 bp plus 300 bp bands in lane Y; full sample DNA lengths are 900 bp. Which statement follows from band positions alone?
options: A) Lane Y contains twice as much DNA as lane X
B) Lane X is necessarily heterozygous
C) Lane Y DNA was cut at one internal position, while X was not cut at that site
D) The 600 bp fragment must fluoresce twice as brightly as the 300 bp band
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) One cut yields the two lengths.
Why: Two Y fragments sum to the starting 900 bp and are compatible with one internal restriction site; uncut X yields the full-length band. Band positions provide fragment lengths, not quantitative mass or genotype without additional lane and intensity context.
Why not the others: (A) band positions alone do not measure total DNA mass; (B) uncut X does not prove a heterozygous genotype; (D) position alone does not establish fluorescence intensity.
Key point: Read fragment sizes, not hidden abundance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The structures show NH₃ and NF₃ with three bonds and one lone pair on central nitrogen. Which has the larger H–N–H or F–N–F bond angle, respectively?
options: A) NH₃, because N–H bond pairs stay nearer N than N–F bond pairs
B) NF₃, because F is larger than H
C) Equal, because both have four domains
D) NF₃, because lone pairs vanish in polar bonds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) NH₃ has the wider angle.
Why: F draws bonding electron density away from N, weakening N-centred bond-pair repulsions relative to the lone pair and compressing F–N–F. Both are trigonal pyramidal, but identical domain count does not imply identical angles.
Why not the others: (B) invokes atomic size alone; (C) overlooks electronegativity; (D) incorrectly removes the lone pair.
Key point: VSEPR angles depend on where bonding density lies.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In an octahedral d⁶ complex, a strong-field ligand gives a low-spin state. How many unpaired electrons are expected?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Zero.
Why: Large octahedral splitting makes pairing in lower t₂g orbitals preferable to promotion into e_g. Six d electrons fill t₂g as three pairs, leaving e_g empty, so all spins are paired.
Why not the others: (A) is a weak-field d⁶ case; (C) misallocates a pair; (D) ignores Pauli pairing and t₂g capacity.
Key point: Compare splitting to pairing energy before filling d levels.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A first-row transition-metal complex has three unpaired electrons. What is its spin-only magnetic moment in Bohr magnetons, approximately?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) √15 BM.
Given: Number of unpaired spins n=3.
Formula/Principle: Spin-only moment μ=√[n(n+2)] BM.
Step 1: μ=√[3(5)]=√15 BM.
Why: The expression counts spin angular-momentum contribution under the stipulated spin-only approximation, not the number of d electrons directly. The square-root expression is an approximation that omits orbital contributions, so the reported unpaired count is the required input.
Why not the others: (A) uses √n; (B) corresponds to n=2; (D) corresponds to n=4.
Key point: Use unpaired count rather than oxidation state alone.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Two electrons are proposed in the same atom with identical (n,l,m_l,m_s) quantum numbers. Which rule rules this out even if the orbital energies are equal?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Pauli exclusion.
Why: A complete set of four identical quantum numbers would specify an identical one-electron state for both electrons. Fermions cannot occupy that same state; opposite spins can share one spatial orbital. Energy degeneracy does not suspend this rule.
Why not the others: (A) concerns filling degenerate orbitals; (B) orders energies; (C) does not state the identical-state occupancy restriction.
Key point: Compare all four quantum numbers.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.question: Among Be, B, N and O in the second period, which paired first-ionisation-energy comparisons are both correct, and what orbital effects explain them?
options: A) Be>B due to starting a 2p electron in B; N>O because paired 2p electrons in O repel
B) B>Be due to greater nuclear charge; O>N due to greater nuclear charge
C) Be>B because Be has a filled 2p shell; N>O because N has no p electrons
D) B>Be because B is more metallic; N>O because O has a half-filled p shell
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both local exceptions are real.
Why: B's first 2p electron is easier to remove than a Be 2s electron despite B's extra proton. N has three singly occupied 2p orbitals; O introduces one paired 2p electron with extra repulsion, lowering its first ionisation energy relative to N. The general across-period increase needs both corrections.
Why not the others: (B) ignores subshell and pairing; (C) misassigns Be and N configurations; (D) reverses metallic character and half-filled stability.
Key point: Apply electron configuration before using a broad periodic trend.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: At identical temperature and pressure, 10 mL of H₂ and 10 mL of O₂ react completely as far as stoichiometry permits, then the water vapour is condensed. Which gas remains and what is its volume at the original T,P?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 5 mL oxygen.
Given: 2H₂+O₂→2H₂O and gas volumes at the same T,P follow mole ratios.
Formula/Principle: 10 mL hydrogen consumes 5 mL oxygen.
Step 1: Oxygen left=10−5=5 mL; product water condenses.
Why: Equal starting gas volumes do not supply the 2:1 hydrogen-to-oxygen ratio required for both to disappear. Condensation removes the product from the gas-volume reading.
Why not the others: (A) hydrogen is completely consumed and cannot leave 10 mL; (C) the same limiting reagent cannot leave 5 mL; (D) assumes equal volumes react despite the 2:1 equation.
Key point: Apply stoichiometric volume ratios before condensation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which acid is stronger in water, CH₃COOH or ClCH₂COOH, and why?
options: A) CH₃COOH because methyl withdraws electrons
B) Equal because both are carboxylic acids
C) ClCH₂COOH because chlorine withdraws electron density inductively and stabilises its conjugate base
D) ClCH₂COOH because it has more resonance structures
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Chloroacetic acid.
Why: Electron withdrawal through sigma bonds stabilises the carboxylate conjugate base relative to unsubstituted acetate. Both conjugate bases have carboxylate resonance; the extra chlorine effect is principally inductive in this pair.
Why not the others: (A) methyl is donating; (B) ignores substituent effects; (D) claims an extra resonance topology absent here.
Key point: Compare conjugate-base stability under matched functional groups.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In aqueous nucleophilic addition of HCN to acetone under suitable conditions, which atom of CN⁻ bonds to the carbonyl carbon in the usual cyanohydrin product?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cyanide carbon.
Why: The nucleophilic carbon end forms the new C–C bond at electrophilic carbonyl carbon; the π electrons move onto oxygen, then protonation gives a hydroxyl group. The resulting cyanohydrin retains a nitrile C≡N bond.
Why not the others: (A) is delivered during protonation; (B) is the pre-existing carbonyl atom; (C) gives the wrong connectivity of the usual product.
Key point: Follow bond formation and protonation separately.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A liquid gives H₂ with sodium metal but no CO₂ with aqueous NaHCO₃. It is soluble in water and has no carbonyl peak. Which class is best supported?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Alcohol.
Why: A protic O–H group can release H₂ with sodium; failure to evolve CO₂ with bicarbonate argues against the stronger carboxylic acid. Water solubility and absent carbonyl are consistent supporting clues, though not a unique structure.
Why not the others: (B) reacts with bicarbonate; (C) has carbonyl; (D) lacks suitable acidic O–H.
Key point: Use positive and negative controls together.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A cold diazonium-salt solution couples with phenol in mildly alkaline medium, but heating its aqueous solution instead replaces the diazonium group by OH. What is the key reason the products differ?
options: A) Phenol is always a reducing agent
B) The reaction partner and thermal conditions select coupling versus hydrolysis
C) The aryl ring vanishes on warming
D) Diazonium salts can form only at high temperature
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Conditions control competing transformations.
Why: Cold alkaline phenol supplies an activated aromatic coupling partner for an azo bond; warming aqueous diazonium promotes N₂ loss and phenolic substitution. A reagent's identity alone does not determine outcome without reaction conditions.
Why not the others: (A) is not the coupling mechanism; (C) the ring remains; (D) reverses diazonium stability.
Key point: Preserve temperature and partner in product prediction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An amino acid has one amino and one carboxyl group, with no ionisable side chain. At pH near its isoelectric point, which species predominates?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Zwitterion.
Why: Proton transfer gives an ammonium group and a carboxylate group carrying opposite charges. At the isoelectric point the average net charge is zero, though equilibrium includes minor other forms.
Why not the others: (A) ignores dominant internal ionisation; (B) is net positive; (D) misstates carboxylate charge.
Key point: Net neutral need not mean absence of charges.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Mixture A–B has a total vapour pressure above its Raoult-law ideal line at an intermediate composition. Which microscopic interaction trend is consistent with this positive deviation?
options: A) A–B attractions are stronger than both pure like-like interactions
B) No molecules escape the liquid
C) A–B bonds are covalent and unbreakable
D) A–B attractions are weaker on average, making escape easier
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Weaker unlike interactions.
Why: Disrupting stronger like-like contacts and forming weaker unlike contacts makes components more prone to enter vapour than ideal prediction, elevating partial and total vapour pressures. The sign of deviation reflects relative intermolecular interactions, not simple gas quantity conservation.
Why not the others: (A) favours negative deviation; (B) predicts zero pressure; (C) contradicts ordinary liquid mixing.
Key point: Compare unlike and like attractions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For a strong electrolyte at fixed temperature, dilution decreases specific conductivity κ but increases molar conductivity Λm toward a limiting value. Which statement explains both?
options: A) Ion concentration per volume falls while conductivity per mole can rise as interactions weaken
B) Ion concentration per volume increases under dilution
C) Each ion loses its charge under dilution
D) Λm must equal κ numerically at every concentration
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Different normalisations give different trends.
Why: Dilution puts fewer charge carriers in each unit volume, lowering κ, while Λm=κ/c measures conductance per mole and can increase as ion mobility is less hindered. The trends need not be identical because their denominators differ.
Why not the others: (B) reverses dilution; (C) denies strong-electrolyte ionisation; (D) ignores units and concentration.
Key point: Distinguish per-volume from per-mole conductance.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A first-order reaction has half-life 20 min. After 60 min, what fraction of initial reactant remains?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/8.
Given: 60 min spans three half-lives.
Formula/Principle: Fraction remaining=(1/2)^(t/t_half).
Step 1: (1/2)³=1/8.
Why: Each equal half-life halves the amount remaining, not a fixed amount of the initial sample. Three successive halvings produce 1/2, 1/4, 1/8.
Why not the others: (A) counts two periods; (B) counts five; (C) counts four.
Key point: Exponential decay counts elapsed half-life intervals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g), the diagram gives an equilibrium mixture with pNO2=2 atm and pN2O4=1 atm, then NO₂ pressure is instantaneously increased to 4 atm at constant T before reaction. Relative to the old equilibrium, which way does reaction initially proceed?
options: A) Right because NO₂ was added
B) No shift because T is unchanged
C) Left because Qp rises from 4 to 16
D) Right because the product pressure is squared
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Left.
Why: Initially Kp=2²/1=4. Immediately after adding NO₂, Qp=4²/1=16>Kp, so net reaction consumes product until quotient falls back toward Kp. Temperature fixes Kp but does not force a disturbed mixture to remain at equilibrium.
Why not the others: (A) treats product addition as a right-driving disturbance; (B) confuses fixed Kp with the temporarily changed Qp; (D) interprets squaring the product pressure in the opposite direction.
Key point: Evaluate Q immediately after a disturbance.
questions.image_alt: Reaction quotient pressure values for the two gases

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A hyperbola has equation x²/9−y²/16=1. What is the acute angle θ that either asymptote makes with the positive x-axis, through tan θ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) tan θ=4/3.
Given: a=3 and b=4.
Formula/Principle: Asymptotes of x²/a²−y²/b²=1 are y=±(b/a)x.
Step 1: Magnitude of slope is 4/3.
Worked derivation: \[0=\frac{x^2}{9}-\frac{y^2}{16}\Rightarrow y=\pm\frac43x,\qquad \tan\theta=\left|\frac yx\right|=\frac43.\]
Why: Asymptote slopes arise by setting the leading quadratic homogeneous part to zero, not from focus distance. The asymptotes are straight lines through the hyperbola's centre, and their rise/run is set by b/a rather than a/b.
Why not the others: (B) inverts slope; (C) uses b/c; (D) uses c/b.
Key point: Read slope b/a for transverse x-axis.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: All lines in the family (2+k)x+(3−k)y=5+k pass through one fixed point. What is that point?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (8/5,3/5).
Given: Equation rearranges as (2x+3y−5)+k(x−y−1)=0.
Formula/Principle: A fixed point satisfies both k-independent and k coefficients equal zero.
Step 1: x−y=1 and 2x+3y=5, giving y=3/5, x=8/5.
Worked derivation: \[x-y-1=0,\quad 2x+3y-5=0\Rightarrow y=\frac35,\ x=\frac85.\]
Why: A point on every member must cancel the k term independently; solving just one chosen k line is insufficient. The resulting point can be checked by substituting it into two distinct members of the line family, confirming it persists for every k.
Why not the others: (A) fails both equalities; (C) has x−y=−1; (D) has x−y=−5/3.
Key point: Separate constant and parameter coefficients.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let f(x)=ax² for x≤1 and f(x)=bx+c for x>1. If f is differentiable at x=1 and f(2)=5, what is c?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −5/3.
Given: Continuity gives a=b+c; equal one-sided slopes give 2a=b; also 2b+c=5.
Formula/Principle: Solve these three linear constraints.
Step 1: c=a−2a=−a; 4a−a=5, so a=5/3, c=−5/3.
Worked derivation: \[a=b+c,\ b=2a,\ 2b+c=5\Rightarrow 3a=5,\quad c=-\frac53.\]
Why: Differentiability requires both matching value and matching derivative; matching only values leaves a free parameter. The third value f(2)=5 fixes the remaining scale after the first two conditions, leading to a negative intercept c.
Why not the others: (A) assumes a=1; (B) uses positive a; (D) treats f(2) as c.
Key point: Use continuity and equal one-sided derivatives.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate ∫₀^π x sin x dx using the symmetry x↔π−x.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) π.
Given: I=∫₀^π x sin x dx.
Formula/Principle: Substitute x↔π−x and add integrals.
Step 1: 2I=π∫₀^π sin x dx=2π, hence I=π.
Worked derivation: \[2I=\int_0^\pi[x+(\pi-x)]\sin x\,dx=\pi\int_0^\pi\sin x\,dx=2\pi\Rightarrow I=\pi.\]
Why: Sine is symmetric around π/2, so complementary x values sum to π. Adding the original and reflected integrals cancels the x-dependence of their coefficients and leaves the simpler sine integral.
Why not the others: (A) halves twice; (B) omits final division; (D) treats integral as normalized.
Key point: Pair complementary arguments.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let f(x)=√(4−x²) and g(x)=1/(x−1). What is the domain of g∘f?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Exclude ±√3.
Worked derivation: \[4-x^2\ge0\Rightarrow -2\le x\le2;\quad f(x)\ne1\Rightarrow\sqrt{4-x^2}\ne1\Rightarrow x\ne\pm\sqrt3.\]
Why: The outer function is undefined when its input equals one, so those two real preimages must be removed from the inner function's allowed interval. Endpoints give f=0 and are permitted.
Why not the others: (A) misses poles; (B) wrongly loses endpoints; (C) solves f(x)=1 incorrectly.
Key point: Impose both inner and outer domains.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A 3×3 determinant D has rows r₁,r₂,r₃. After replacing r₂ by r₂+3r₁ and interchanging r₁ with r₃, the result is −10. What is D?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10.
Given: Adding a multiple of a row to another preserves determinant.
Formula/Principle: One row interchange reverses determinant sign.
Step 1: New determinant=−D=−10.
Worked derivation: \[D'=\det(r_3,r_2+3r_1,r_1)=-D=-10\Rightarrow D=10.\]
Why: The addition does not contribute a factor three; only the swap changes the determinant. Reversing the sequence of operations gives the same sign conclusion only if the row addition is tracked on the correct current rows.
Why not the others: (A) multiplies by three and flips; (B) ignores swap; (D) multiplies by three.
Key point: Apply row-operation effects sequentially.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Factory A supplies 70% and B 30% of devices. Defect rates are 2% and 6% respectively. A randomly chosen device is defective. What is the probability it came from B?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 9/16.
Given: Joint defective B=0.30×0.06=0.018; defective A=0.70×0.02=0.014.
Formula/Principle: Bayes posterior=joint B-defective / total defective.
Step 1: 0.018/(0.018+0.014)=18/32=9/16.
Worked derivation: \[P(B\mid D)=\frac{0.3(0.06)}{0.7(0.02)+0.3(0.06)}=\frac{9}{16}.\]
Why: Conditioning on a defect changes factory weights; using 30% alone ignores different defect rates. A defective sample is disproportionately likely to come from B because its defect rate is three times A's, despite B's smaller production share.
Why not the others: (A) uses an incorrect posterior ratio; (C) omits part of the total defective probability; (D) treats the two sources as equally likely after observing a defect.
Key point: Weight both priors before normalization.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: In (x+2)⁶, what is the ratio of the coefficient of x³ to the coefficient of x⁴?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8/3.
Given: Coefficient x³=C(6,3)2³=160; x⁴=C(6,4)2²=60.
Formula/Principle: Binomial theorem with x powers tracked by chosen k.
Step 1: 160/60=8/3.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\binom63 2^3}{\binom64 2^2}=\frac{20\cdot8}{15\cdot4}=\frac83.\]
Why: The exponent of 2 is the complement of the exponent of x, so adjacent coefficients contain both binomial and power factors. Taking only the ratio of binomial coefficients loses the extra factor of two from the different powers of the constant term.
Why not the others: (A) uses only powers; (B) uses binomial ratio alone; (C) rounds.
Key point: Track both factors in each term.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For 0<r<1 let S=1+2r+3r²+⋯=4. What is the alternating companion sum T=1−2r+3r²−4r³+⋯?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4/9.
Given: For |z|<1, ∑(n+1)zⁿ=1/(1−z)².
Formula/Principle: First solve S=1/(1−r)², then evaluate the same series at z=−r.
Step 1: 0<r<1 gives 1−r>0, hence r=1/2.
Worked derivation: \[\frac1{(1-r)^2}=4\Rightarrow r=\frac12,\qquad T=\frac1{(1+r)^2}=\frac1{(3/2)^2}=\frac49.\]
Why: Alternating signs correspond to replacing r by −r in the generating function; they do not negate the entire sum. The stated convergence interval justifies both substitutions.
Why not the others: (A) squares 1/(1+r) again; (B) assumes T=1/S; (D) omits the square.
Key point: Use one generating function for two related series.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let f(x)=sin(kx)/x for nonzero x and f(0)=2. For which real k is f continuous at x=0?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2.
Given: k is a constant and sin(kx)/(kx) tends to 1 as x tends to zero.
Formula/Principle: Continuity requires limₓ→₀f(x)=f(0).
Step 1: sin(kx)/x=k[sin(kx)/(kx)] tends to k (including k=0 by direct evaluation).
Worked derivation: \[\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\sin(kx)}{x}=k,\qquad k=f(0)=2.\]
Why: The parameter controls the limiting slope of sine near zero; cancellation of an algebraic factor is not the method here. The same limit holds for negative k by the scaled sine limit, but only k=2 matches the explicitly assigned value at zero.
Why not the others: (A) gives limit −2; (B) gives zero; (C) gives one.
Key point: Use the standard trigonometric limit with its scale factor.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the foot of perpendicular from P=(3,4) to the line 3x+4y−10=0.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (6/5,8/5).
Given: Normal vector n=(3,4), n·P−10=15.
Formula/Principle: Foot H=P−[(n·P−10)/norm(n)²]n.
Step 1: Subtract (15/25)(3,4)=(9/5,12/5) from P, giving (6/5,8/5).
Worked derivation: \[H=(3,4)-\frac{15}{25}(3,4)=\left(\frac65,\frac85\right).\]
Why: The correction vector is along the line's normal; its endpoint, not the correction itself, is the foot. Because the point P itself does not lie on the line, returning the displacement vector would confuse a direction-and-length with a coordinate.
Why not the others: (A) projects onto y-axis; (C) reports correction; (D) fails line equation.
Key point: Subtract the normal displacement from P.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A path from (0,0) to (4,4) uses only right and up steps. How many paths pass through exactly one of A=(1,2) and B=(3,2)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 42.
Given: Paths via A: C(3,1)C(5,2)=30; via B: C(5,2)C(3,1)=30. Paths via both: C(3,1)C(2,0)C(3,1)=9.
Formula/Principle: Exactly one=through A+through B−2(through both).
Step 1: 30+30−18=42.
Worked derivation: \[N_{\rm exactly\ one}=\binom31\binom52+\binom52\binom31-2\binom31\binom20\binom31=42.\]
Why: A path visiting both checkpoints appears in each individual through count and must be removed twice to satisfy exactly one. The order A then B is possible but B then A is impossible with only right/up steps, which makes the double-visit product unambiguous.
Why not the others: (A) keeps double visits twice; (C) removes them once; (D) counts only double visits.
Key point: Correct double-counting for an exclusive condition.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A polynomial with real coefficients has 2+i as a root. Which statement must be true?
options: C) Its degree is exactly two
D) Its constant term is positive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The conjugate is a root.
Worked derivation: \[P(2+i)=0,\quad P(2-i)=\overline{P(2+i)}=0\qquad(P\in\mathbb R[x]).\]
Why: Real coefficients commute with complex conjugation, forcing nonreal roots to occur in conjugate pairs. The remaining roots or leading coefficient are unrestricted.
Why not the others: (B) is not conjugation; (C) allows higher degree; (D) depends on other roots and leading coefficient.
Key point: Conjugate-root theorem requires real coefficients.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Solve dy/dx=(x+y)/x for x>0, given y(1)=0. What is y(e)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) e.
Given: Set v=y/x, so y=xv and y′=v+xv′.
Formula/Principle: Equation becomes v+xv′=1+v, hence v′=1/x.
Step 1: v=ln x+C; y(1)=0 gives C=0; y(e)=e.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dv}{dx}=\frac1x,\quad y=x\ln x,\quad y(e)=e\ln e=e.\]
Why: The homogeneous substitution removes the y/x term and the initial condition fixes the integration constant. Substituting x=e only after finding the full solution preserves the initial-value constant and avoids treating v as y.
Why not the others: (B) omits factor x; (C) squares x; (D) subtracts a spurious constant.
Key point: Use y=xv for a homogeneous first-order equation.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: If sin θ+cos θ=1/2 for real θ, what is sin 2θ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −3/4.
Given: Square the given identity.
Formula/Principle: (sin θ+cos θ)²=1+sin2θ.
Step 1: 1/4=1+sin2θ.
Worked derivation: \[\sin2\theta=(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2-1=\frac14-1=-\frac34.\]
Why: The stipulated sum fixes sin2θ even though many distinct θ satisfy it; squaring is sufficient for this requested invariant. The real angle need not be found explicitly; the given sum already determines the double-angle invariant via the Pythagorean identity.
Why not the others: (B) treats product incorrectly; (C) omits −1; (D) loses sign.
Key point: Squared sum directly contains double-angle sine.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A displacement obeys x=At²+B sin(ωt), where x is length and t is time. What are dimensions of A and B, respectively?
options: A) L T⁻¹ and L T⁻²
D) L T⁻² and L T
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) L T⁻² and L.
Worked derivation: \[[At^2]=L\Rightarrow[A]=LT^{-2};\quad [\sin(\omega t)]=1\Rightarrow[B]=L.\]
Why: Arguments of trig functions must be dimensionless, hence ωt has no dimension; each additive term of x separately has dimension length. B must carry length because it multiplies a dimensionless sine, even though the oscillation frequency has units of inverse time.
Why not the others: (A) assigns velocity to A; (C) ignores time factor; (D) treats sine as a time quantity.
Key point: Check each sum term and trig argument.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two blocks of masses m and 2m are connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley. What is acceleration magnitude when released?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) g/3.
Given: Net driving force is (2m−m)g=mg; total accelerated mass 3m.
Formula/Principle: Combine two Newton equations, eliminating tension.
Step 1: a=mg/(3m)=g/3.
Worked derivation: \[2mg-T=2ma,\quad T-mg=ma\Rightarrow mg=3ma\Rightarrow a=\frac g3.\]
Why: Tension is internal to the two-block system; subtract weights but add masses to compute acceleration. If only the heavier block's mass were used in the denominator, the shared string would be accelerating an omitted second block.
Why not the others: (A) uses an incorrect total mass; (B) overcounts inertia; (D) treats the net driving weight as 2mg.
Key point: Keep drive and inertia distinct.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two wires of equal material and length, with cross-sectional areas A and 2A, are connected in series and pulled by force F. What is extension of the narrower wire divided by extension of the wider one?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2.
Given: Series tension F is the same in both wires.
Formula/Principle: Extension ΔL=FL/(YA).
Step 1: Halving area doubles extension at fixed F,L,Y.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\Delta L_A}{\Delta L_{2A}}=\frac{FL/(YA)}{FL/(2YA)}=2.\]
Why: A series connection shares force, not extension; the thinner wire has twice the strain under equal material and length. This ratio remains unchanged when both wires are stretched more strongly, as long as they stay in the linear elastic regime.
Why not the others: (A) reverses ratio; (B) assumes equal extension; (C) squares area ratio.
Key point: Force is common through series wires.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A metal rod fits exactly between two rigid supports at 20°C. Temperature rises by ΔT while supports stay fixed and the rod remains elastic. What is the magnitude of compressive stress, if its Young modulus is Y and expansion coefficient α?
options: D) Zero because length is fixed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) YαΔT.
Given: Free thermal strain would be +αΔT; actual total strain is zero.
Formula/Principle: Mechanical compressive strain must be −αΔT, with magnitude stress/Y.
Step 1: |σ|/Y=αΔT.
Worked derivation: \[0=\epsilon_{\rm mech}+\alpha\Delta T\Rightarrow \epsilon_{\rm mech}=-\alpha\Delta T,\quad |\sigma|=Y\alpha\Delta T.\]
Why: Constraints prevent geometric expansion but produce internal compression rather than eliminating thermal tendency. The Young modulus relates the compensating mechanical strain to stress, so a higher modulus generates a larger force under the same restraint.
Why not the others: (B) divides by α incorrectly; (C) inverts Y rather than multiplying it; (D) mistakes fixed length for absence of thermal stress.
Key point: Add thermal and mechanical strains.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A diatomic ideal gas has rotations active but vibrations frozen in the listed temperature range. If its measured molar CV is near 5R/2, what is expected molar CP?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 7R/2.
Given: Ideal-gas Mayer relation CP−CV=R.
Formula/Principle: CV=5R/2 under the stated active degrees of freedom.
Step 1: CP=5R/2+R=7R/2.
Worked derivation: \[C_P=C_V+R=\frac{5R}{2}+R=\frac{7R}{2}.\]
Why: The extra R accounts for pressure-volume work during constant-pressure heating, not an additional internal mode. The stipulated frozen vibrational modes prevent adding another thermal degree-of-freedom term to the internal energy.
Why not the others: (A) removes R; (C) equates heat capacities; (D) adds two R.
Key point: Keep active modes and process work separate.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: At a point on a circular path with constant speed, velocity points east. Which direction does acceleration point if the centre is north of that point?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) North, toward centre.
Worked derivation: \[\vec a=\frac{v^2}{r}\,\hat{\mathbf r}_{\rm inward},\quad |\vec v|=\text{constant but }d\vec v/dt\ne0.\]
Why: The velocity vector changes direction despite unchanged magnitude, producing inward centripetal acceleration. Its direction is fixed by the centre's position, not by motion direction.
Why not the others: (A) east is the instantaneous velocity direction, not acceleration; (B) west is the opposite tangent; (D) confuses unchanging speed with unchanging velocity vector.
Key point: Acceleration describes change of vector velocity.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A wave on a string reaches a boundary with a much denser string, while the incident pulse is upward. What is the direction of the reflected pulse close to a fixed-end limit?
options: A) Upward with no phase reversal
D) Downward due to approximate π phase reversal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Inverted pulse.
Worked derivation: \[r_{\rm amplitude}\to-1\quad\text{as the load approaches a fixed boundary};\quad \Delta\phi=\pi.\]
Why: To keep the junction displacement small in a fixed-end limit, incident and reflected displacements nearly cancel at the boundary; that demands opposite signs. The limiting reflected pulse travels back in the lighter string with reversed displacement even though its direction of propagation also reverses.
Why not the others: (A) describes free-end reflection; (B) ignores impedance mismatch; (C) wrongly extends boundary condition to entire string.
Key point: Use displacement boundary condition to infer phase.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.question: A closed spherical Gaussian surface encloses +q and −3q; a +5q charge sits just outside it. What is the total electric flux through the sphere?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −2q/ε₀.
Given: Enclosed net charge is +q−3q=−2q.
Formula/Principle: Gauss law ΦE=Qenc/ε₀.
Step 1: Exclude external +5q from enclosed total.
Worked derivation: \[\Phi_E=\frac{q-3q}{\epsilon_0}=-\frac{2q}{\epsilon_0}.\]
Why: External charge alters local field crossing parts of the sphere, but its inward and outward contributions cancel in the net closed-surface flux. The sign is negative because the enclosed negative charge has greater magnitude than the enclosed positive charge.
Why not the others: (B) takes magnitude of one charge; (C) uses outside charge; (D) omits +q.
Key point: Closed flux depends on enclosed net charge.
questions.image_alt: Closed surface and inside/outside charge positions

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A network has R between A and B, another R between B and C, and a direct resistor 2R from A to C. Ideal wires make B a distinct node. What is equivalent resistance between A and C?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) R.
Given: Series A–B–C branch totals 2R; direct A–C branch is 2R.
Formula/Principle: Two equal 2R branches in parallel give R.
Step 1: Req=(2R)(2R)/(2R+2R)=R.
Worked derivation: \[R_{\rm eq}=(R+R)\parallel 2R=\left(\frac1{2R}+\frac1{2R}\right)^{-1}=R.\]
Why: The intermediate B node has no other branch, allowing its two resistors in series; both resulting paths share endpoints A and C. This reduction remains valid because B is not shorted to A or C by another ideal wire, as the diagram explicitly shows.
Why not the others: (B) treats all three parallel; (C) ignores parallel path; (D) adds both branches.
Key point: Identify nodes before combining resistors.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A circular loop is viewed face-on. A magnetic field into the page increases in magnitude. Which direction is induced conventional current?
options: D) No induced current because field direction stays fixed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Counterclockwise.
Worked derivation: \[\mathcal E=-\frac{d\Phi_B}{dt};\quad \text{increasing inward flux}\Rightarrow\text{induced outward field}.\]
Why: Lenz's law opposes the change in flux, not necessarily the original field. By right-hand grip rule, a counterclockwise loop current makes an outward magnetic field as viewed face-on.
Why not the others: (A) aids change; (C) mismatches current and field; (D) ignores changing magnitude.
Key point: Determine opposing field before current direction.
questions.image_alt: Increasing inward flux through the loop

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: In a series AC circuit with R=6 Ω, XL=10 Ω and XC=2 Ω at the drive frequency, what is impedance magnitude?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 10 Ω.
Given: Net reactance XL−XC=8 Ω.
Formula/Principle: Series impedance magnitude Z=√[R²+(XL−XC)²].
Step 1: √(36+64)=10 Ω.
Worked derivation: \[Z=\sqrt{6^2+(10-2)^2}=\sqrt{100}=10\ \Omega.\]
Why: Inductive and capacitive voltages oppose in phase; their reactances subtract before combining quadratically with resistance. At the selected frequency the inductor dominates the capacitor by 8 Ω, but that 8 Ω is reactive and cannot be added arithmetically to 6 Ω.
Why not the others: (A) ignores resistance; (B) adds R and reactance; (D) adds all impedances.
Key point: Reactances subtract; resistance is perpendicular in phasor space.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A thin converging lens of focal length 20 cm forms a real image of an object 30 cm in front of it. A plane mirror is placed exactly at the image plane, perpendicular to the axis. Where do returned rays form the final image after passing back through the lens?
options: B) 30 cm on the object side
C) 20 cm on the object side
D) 60 cm on the mirror side
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 30 cm on original object side.
Given: The first pass images the object at 60 cm; the mirror at this plane reflects rays that then diverge from that same axial point toward the lens.
Formula/Principle: For the return pass, a point 60 cm from the lens is conjugate to a point 30 cm from it.
Step 1: Solve the thin-lens relation on each pass, with the direction of light reversed on return.
Worked derivation: \[\frac1{20}=\frac1{30}+\frac1{60};\quad \frac1{20}=\frac1{60}+\frac1{30}\Rightarrow u_{\rm final}=30\ {\rm cm\ on\ object\ side}.\]
Why: The point on the mirror plane becomes the object point for the return traversal. A plane mirror reverses the axial component of each ray, but oblique rays need not retrace their individual incident lines; the lens still forms the conjugate point on the original object side.
Why not the others: (A) a finite-distance object does not produce an image on the lens plane; (C) confuses the focal length with the conjugate image distance; (D) leaves the answer on the mirror side despite the return through the lens.
Key point: Treat the mirror-plane point as the source for the return pass.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two coherent beams of equal intensities interfere at a screen. One beam's intensity is reduced to one quarter while coherence and phase stability remain unchanged. What is fringe visibility V=(Imax−Imin)/(Imax+Imin)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4/5.
Given: Beam amplitudes scale as square roots of intensity, so amplitude ratio becomes 1:1/2.
Formula/Principle: Visibility=2√(I₁I₂)/(I₁+I₂).
Step 1: With intensities 1 and 1/4, V=1/(5/4)=4/5.
Worked derivation: \[V=\frac{2\sqrt{1\cdot(1/4)}}{1+1/4}=\frac1{5/4}=\frac45.\]
Why: Contrast remains nonzero but falls below unity for unequal intensities. Attenuation changes amplitude, not the stated coherence.
Why not the others: (A) uses amplitude ratio; (B) uses intensity ratio; (C) assumes equal intensities.
Key point: Visibility depends on both beam amplitudes.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.question: An electron and a proton each start from rest and are accelerated through the same potential difference V. What is the ratio of their nonrelativistic de Broglie wavelengths λe/λp?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) √(mp/me).
Given: Each gains kinetic energy eV of equal magnitude.
Formula/Principle: p=√(2m eV) and λ=h/p.
Step 1: λ∝1/√m at fixed V and charge magnitude.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_p}=\frac{h/\sqrt{2m_e eV}}{h/\sqrt{2m_p eV}}=\sqrt{\frac{m_p}{m_e}}.\]
Why: Equal energy does not mean equal momentum; the lighter electron acquires smaller momentum and longer wavelength. The nonrelativistic condition matters because at sufficiently high accelerating voltage the momentum-energy relation would no longer be √(2meV).
Why not the others: (B) inverts; (C) omits square root; (D) assumes equal mass.
Key point: Compare momentum at equal kinetic energy.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The diode I–V plot has nearly zero forward current up to about 0.6 V, then a sharp rise; reverse current remains small until a large negative voltage. Which operating point best corresponds to ordinary forward conduction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) +0.8 V, high forward current.
Worked derivation: \[V=+0.8\ {\rm V}>0.6\ {\rm V}\Rightarrow\text{point lies on steep positive-current branch}.\]
Why: The graph itself locates the approximate turn-on region; at +0.8 V the forward-bias branch has risen markedly. A small reverse bias does not produce large positive current.
Why not the others: (A) small reverse bias does not give large forward current; (B) +0.2 V is below the depicted rise; (C) −0.8 V remains on the small reverse-current branch shown.
Key point: Read operating regime from the labelled plot.
questions.image_alt: Forward and reverse diode current-voltage plot
